summary: Defines enhancements to NNTP that allow a client to request more information from a server about its status and policy, through new keywords for the LIST command from RFC 3977. It also updates and formalizes the LIST DISTRIB.PATS keyword.

plainLanguage.summary: Usenet news servers can answer "what do you have?" questions. This adds new questions clients can ask about the server's settings and rules.

questions: what does nntp group status x j mean
subtitle: Five new LIST variants and three new group status values let news clients ask servers about policy and configuration.

tldr.problem: Several LIST variants were in use with limited or no documentation, and the LIST ACTIVE status values defined for NNTP only covered local posting rights, not how a server handles articles from peers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds the LIST keywords COUNTS, DISTRIBUTIONS, MODERATORS, MOTD and SUBSCRIPTIONS, advertised through the LIST capability, and defines status values x, j and =newsgroup for LIST ACTIVE.
tldr.outcome: It formalizes the DISTRIBUTIONS and SUBSCRIPTIONS commands from RFC 2980 and updates RFC 2980 and RFC 3977. Where it conflicts with RFC 3977, RFC 3977 takes precedence.

today: RFC 6048 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2980 and RFC 3977. According to the metadata for this site, no later RFC has obsoleted or updated it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The NNTP base specification, RFC 3977, defines the LIST capability and keywords such as ACTIVE, ACTIVE.TIMES, DISTRIB.PATS, HEADERS, NEWSGROUPS and OVERVIEW.FMT. Other LIST variants were in use but poorly documented, and this memo formalizes them.

DISTRIBUTIONS and SUBSCRIPTIONS were first documented in RFC 2980. MOTD came from an earlier draft document, and COUNTS and MODERATORS had not been documented before. The memo should be read together with RFC 3977, which takes precedence in a conflict.
sections.plainLanguage: Some useful questions news programs could ask servers were never written down properly. This document writes them down.

sections.title: Advertising the New Variants
sections.content:
Each new keyword is OPTIONAL. A server that supports a variant advertises the keyword on the LIST line of its CAPABILITIES response, for example LIST ACTIVE NEWSGROUPS SUBSCRIPTIONS. An advertised keyword MUST have the meaning given in this RFC.

An empty response means the server maintains the information but it is voluntarily empty. If the software implements the variant but this particular server does not maintain the information, the server MUST return response code 503. Variants that take no argument MUST return 501 if one is given.
sections.plainLanguage: A server first lists the extra questions it can answer. An empty answer means there is nothing to say, and a special error means it does not keep that information.

sections.title: The Five New LIST Variants
sections.content:
LIST COUNTS is like LIST ACTIVE but adds an estimated article count. Each line has five fields separated by spaces: group name, high water mark, low water mark, estimated number of articles, and status. Note the high and low marks are in the opposite order to the 211 response to GROUP. It takes an optional wildmat.

LIST DISTRIBUTIONS returns each known distribution and a short description. Clients can use the names as values of the Distribution header field. Descriptions MUST be UTF-8, and a server that implements it SHOULD also implement LIST DISTRIB.PATS.

LIST MODERATORS returns lines of the form wildmat, colon, submission address template. The first matching line is used, so specific patterns come before general ones. If the template contains %s, the server replaces it with the group name with periods changed to dashes, and %% becomes %.

LIST MOTD returns a free-form message of the day from the administrator, which MUST be UTF-8. No timestamp is provided, and a client MAY cache it but MUST NOT rely on cached results.

LIST SUBSCRIPTIONS returns recommended newsgroups in order of importance, most important first. A client SHOULD use a non-empty list in place of a hard-coded default list when first connecting. It takes an optional wildmat.
sections.plainLanguage: Five new questions: how many articles are in each group, what are the regions, who approves posts, what is today's notice, and which groups should a newcomer join.

sections.title: New LIST ACTIVE Status Values
sections.content:
RFC 3977 defines three status values for LIST ACTIVE: y, n and m. This RFC adds three case-sensitive values that describe how a server treats articles arriving from peers. A server SHOULD use them when those meanings are needed and MUST NOT use them for anything else.

  • x: postings and articles from peers are not permitted, so the group is closed.
  • j: only articles from peers are permitted and none are locally filed. An article not crossposted to a valid group is not filed but is still propagated. A server MAY file it under a catch-all group, which SHOULD be named junk.
  • =other.group: only articles from peers are permitted, and they are filed under other.group. This makes the group an alias, typically used during a rename or to correct a misspelled name.

An alias SHOULD NOT point to a moderated newsgroup, since unapproved articles would bypass moderation. It SHOULD NOT point to itself or another alias, and the Newsgroups header field of arriving articles MUST NOT be altered.
sections.plainLanguage: Shelves can be closed, can be a pass-through that sends books elsewhere, or can be a sign saying that these books now live on another shelf.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content:
The RFC gives ABNF (RFC 5234) that extends the list-arguments, newsgroup-status and list-content rules from RFC 3977. For example, COUNTS and SUBSCRIPTIONS take an optional wildmat, while DISTRIBUTIONS, MODERATORS and MOTD take no argument.

A counts line is a newsgroup name followed by three article numbers and a status. The RFC notes that the estimated article count usually has no leading zeros but MAY have them.
sections.plainLanguage: This part is the exact grammar rulebook so that every program writes and reads these lines the same way.

sections.title: Security and Internationalization
sections.content:
The RFC says no new security considerations are introduced beyond those in RFC 3977 and the Netnews architecture document, RFC 5537. It names distribution leakage and e-mail denial of service during moderation as especially relevant.

There are no new internationalization considerations either. Newsgroup names SHOULD be restricted to US-ASCII, while distribution descriptions and the message of the day MUST be in UTF-8.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new to worry about beyond the old rules. Text for people must be written in a standard way that handles many languages.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The RFC gives the registration details for the extension. It extends the LIST capability label with five arguments: COUNTS, DISTRIBUTIONS, MODERATORS, MOTD and SUBSCRIPTIONS. The new commands can be pipelined, and the extension does not alter the capabilities list, command length limits or the effect of MODE READER.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule book gets an official entry that lists the five new questions.

viz.caption: LIST ACTIVE STATUS VALUES (RFC 3977 plus RFC 6048)

items.label: Moderated
items.desc: Postings are forwarded to the moderator. Defined in RFC 3977.

items.label: Closed
items.desc: Postings and articles from peers are not permitted.

items.label: Peers only, not filed
items.desc: Only articles from peers; no articles are locally filed.

items.label: Alias
items.desc: Articles from peers are filed under the named group.
